content: 1Q26 Wrap: Volatile Near Term; Compelling Medium Term

The earnings season confirmed that the disruption is working through the integrated model: downstream and trading drove beats, while upstream strength should become more visible in 2Q. "Wait-and-see" message on distributions, but these too should grind higher as balance sheets improve.
Earnings beat on elevated expectations, driven primarily by downstream margins and trading/optimisation gains.
1Q upstream pricing remained muted by contractual lags; stronger realised pricing should support 2Q earnings materially.
Distribution frameworks remained conservative: companies preferred balance-sheet strengthening over accelerating payouts.
We remain constructive on the sector as higher-for-longer commodity pricing supports FCF and future shareholder returns.
Stick to TotalEnergies (Top Pick) as our preferred quality compounder; BP as the higher-leverage play on FCF improvement; Repsol on refining strength.

Stronger-than-expected 1Q, but the key debate shifts to durability and timing

The European majors entered 1Q26 with expectations already elevated. Consensus earnings had repriced sharply higher into results as commodity prices strengthened, while Energy equities materially outperformed the broader market.
Against that backdrop, the sector still delivered earnings beats.

Contrary to intuition, however, the dominant driver was not upstream prices - instead, most earnings beats came from downstream and trading. That distinction is relevant for how we think about 2Q26 and beyond.
The 1Q26 earnings season signals three things in our view:
- Integrated models continue to monetise disruption through trading and optimisation
- The full upstream pricing benefit from the stronger commodity environment has not yet flowed through to earnings
- Management teams remain cautious on distributions despite stronger cash generation, preferring to preserve balance-sheet flexibility
The implication is that 1Q26 likely marks the start of a broader earnings and distributions uplift rather than the peak.
Earnings beats on top of elevated expectations – driven by downstream and trading
Across the peer group, results generally exceeded expectations despite a significantly higher pre-results bar. The dominant drivers for the earnings beats were downstream and trading.

Downstream, refineries capitalised on the loss of Middle Eastern supply as well as on regional crude and product dislocations. Assets ran exceptionally hard over the quarter, and margins sustained strong levels despite weaker months in January and February – which suggests a strong exit rate out of March into 2Q.
Shell, BP and Eni were the clearest examples of this dynamic.

- BP reported adjusted earnings 20% ahead of consensus, with the beat overwhelmingly driven by Customers & Products, where operating profit exceeded expectations by ~30% due to refining, midstream and exceptional oil trading performance. Its upstream and LNG divisions missed expectations by ~8%.

- Shell similarly beat consensus by 8% through a combination of strong trading, refining and marketing prints, with Chemicals & Products and Marketing beating expectations by a combined 35%, while Integrated Gas missed by more than 10%.

- Eni effectively demonstrated the opposite dynamic, reinforcing where the earnings upside actually came from in 1Q. While upstream performed well – production grew 9% Y/Y – the company missed expectations because outages in two major refineries (Ruwais and Sannazzaro) prevented it from capturing the March refining margin rally, combined with weaker LNG/Power results.
Exhibit 3: Downstream results - including refining, crude/products trading, and marketing - accounted for most of the earnings beat in 1Q26, with muted prints elsewhere
Source: Company data, MS. Note: segment fit across Upstream, IG/LNG, Power, Downstream is indicative; specific company disclosures may not fit exactly across either vertical.

The globally and vertically integrated model proved highly effective in monetising disruption. However, this also raises the key question for the next few quarters: how repeatable are current trading gains?

Our estimate is that trading and optimisation likely contributed some \$3bn in incremental Q/Q earnings in the first quarter – or several hundred million dollars each of Shell, BP and TotalEnergies – particularly across oil and refined products. That would make the strong trading print responsible for nearly half of the earnings growth across the three names, compared to the previous quarter.
That contribution is unlikely to disappear in 2Q, but sustaining 1Q run-rates may well be challenging.

In other words, the sector likely remains structurally supported by disruption – but the composition of earnings should, at the margin, rotate back toward upstream pricing leverage, even if refining continues to do well.

Production and pricing impacts shift into 2Q – with pricing still dominating the net effect

At first glance, output in 1Q26 appeared surprisingly resilient. Oil and gas production across the majors was broadly flat quarter-on-quarter despite material portfolio exposure to the Middle East Gulf. This resilience reflected two offsetting mechanisms:
• disruption effects were felt for only one-third of the quarter
- organic portfolio growth across the group offset part of the disruption

On aggregate, we estimate the majors to have \(\sim 10\%\) aggregate production exposure to Middle East shut-ins in 2Q; with low- to mid-single-digit underlying annual organic growth, the net effect is likely to be a \(\sim 5\%\) production decline compared to the same quarter of last year.
Indeed, companies are now broadly guiding for lower production quarter-on-quarter as disruption impacts become more fully reflected, and maintenance activity increases.
- TotalEnergies indicated that current shut-ins in Qatar, Iraq and UAE offshore represent around 15% of total production exposure.
- BP guided to lower reported upstream production in 2026 due to Gulf of America maintenance and Middle East disruption effects.
- Equinor is expected to see lower production in 2Q despite effectively no Middle East exposure, primarily due to turnaround activity

However, we maintain that the more important variable here remains pricing. The commodity backdrop strengthened materially through the quarter, but the realised benefit in 1Q earnings was still relatively muted.
This reflects contractual pricing lags, weaker January-February pricing, and potentially realised discounts versus spot benchmarks.

As a result, realised pricing across the group lagged the move in spot commodities by roughly $5/bbl across the peer group. The stronger commodity environment should therefore become much more visible in 2Q realised earnings.
At the commodity level, our estimates imply roughly \(\sim 40\%\) quarter-on-quarter improvement in realised upstream pricing assumptions entering 2Q26 versus 1Q26.

The key uncertainty is whether realised prices continue to trade at wider-than-normal discounts to benchmarks due to timing lags, regional pricing distortions or transportation/logistics costs, for instance.

Even so, the broader conclusion remains unchanged: production losses are localised and operationally visible. Pricing benefits are global and apply across entire portfolios. On balance, this asymmetry remains structurally positive for sector earnings.
Exhibit 5: 2Q26 is where a stronger commodity backdrop should really shine through in the earnings of the European majors
Conservative distributions despite materially improved cash generation
The strongest message out of this earnings season was, in our view, a remarkably conservative stance on capital allocation.

The majors' existing capital frameworks were set ahead of a significantly weaker commodity outlook, with the sector preparing for a period of large oil and gas surpluses: capex budgets were tightened, distributions were rebased, and divestment and cost savings programmes became the norm.
Now, despite a higher earnings run-rate and a stronger commodity outlook, companies did not alter frameworks beyond what already existed.
Where flexibility was already embedded in frameworks, they moved toward the higher end of existing ranges:
- TotalEnergies maintained buybacks at the top-end of the range (\$1.5bn/qtr) while reiterating payout discipline
- Eni raised 2026 buybacks guidance to €2.8bn, effectively increasing its planning scenario to $80/bbl oil prices and €50/MWh TTF.
But, importantly, neither company moved beyond their pre-existing distribution frameworks.
Elsewhere, distributions were unchanged – or even lowered:
- BP reiterated its buyback pause and prioritised accelerated de-leveraging
- Equinor maintained its buyback and dividend unchanged, flagging that changes ought to be made on "money already earned" as opposed to stronger forecasts
- Shell notably increased its dividend by a surprise +5% Q/Q, but reduced its buyback to $3.0bn/qtr, effectively trimming annual distributions paid by ~$1.5bn
The message from management teams was very consistent: companies remain cautious about over-distributing into a highly volatile commodity environment.
In practice, the sector is taking a deliberate wait-and-see approach, and management teams appear comfortable allowing additional cash to accumulate on balance sheets in the near term.

However, increases in distributions are a question of "when", not "if", in our view. In a higher-for-longer commodity price environment, current dividend and buyback run-rates might be simply insufficient to meet existing policy floors at ~35-40% of CFFO returned to shareholders.

In our commodity strip (Exhibit 6), we expect CFFO payout policies to be cleared at around $4bn for Shell, $2bn for TotalEnergies and €775mn for Eni (without accounting for a potential special dividend). This would mark a ~30% increase from current run-rates, likely to come before the end of the year.

While Equinor and BP don't have such explicit mechanisms, an increase in returns in the peer group would likely cause them to follow, as they sit on an improved balance sheet and struggle to remain competitive on distributions.

In summary, despite the conservative message out of 1Q26, our expectation for a step-up in buybacks remains unchanged. As the situation remains volatile, management teams have chosen to build balance sheet dry powder – at some point, however, this is likely to translate into higher distributions capacity.

Unstable Near Term, Compelling Medium Term: Sector View Remains 'Attractive'

Near term, the Energy sector is likely to remain volatile. Oil prices and share prices remain closely tied to developments in the Middle East, and the path of the conflict remains difficult to forecast. However, the market is not the same one it was before the disruption started.
Even under a further de-escalation scenario, we do not think investors can simply return

to treating disruption through the Strait of Hormuz as a remote tail risk. Flows remain severely curtailed, inventories have drawn, freight and product markets have repriced, and the market now needs to assign a more persistent risk premium to the new order around the Strait.

That matters for the commodity framework. In oil, we continue to see \$80/bbl as a conservative long-term anchor rather than an aggressive assumption for the coming years. It is close to the most frequently observed real Brent price over the last two decades and remains well below the higher-price regimes associated with demand destruction.

At the same time, perceptions of the level of globally accessible spare capacity have likely shifted lower, strategic stockpiling demand should become an additional source of demand over time, and secure non-Hormuz barrels should command a greater premium. This supports our view that the current backdrop should drive a structural repricing of oil-market risk, not just a cyclical price spike.
Exhibit 9: In our models we assume $80/bbl from 2027, which strikes us a conservative assumption

We also have a constructive view on natural gas. As we argued in Calm on the Surface, storage refill is already lagging and Europe likely needs to price more aggressively into 3Q26 to attract LNG and rebuild inventories. We therefore see further upside risk to both European and global gas prices through year-end, with our forecasts above the forward curve for summer and winter 2026/27.
Exhibit 10: Consensus has not yet fully adjusted to a higher-for-longer oil price on equity models

For equities, the near term will probably remain unsettled, but the medium-term setup is attractive: at \$80+/bbl, the sector works. Cash flow generation remains strong, balance sheets continue to improve, and distribution capacity is still not fully reflected in
Consensus oil price assumptions in equity models

On earnings estimates, we are currently ~10% above consensus compiled by Visible Alpha for 2026, whereas historically we have typically been 5-10% below consensus on the European Energy majors. That represents a meaningful shift in the earnings setup, and we think consensus remains slow to fully reflect the higher commodity price framework.

We also see scope for further upside to consensus buyback forecasts over the coming quarters. The Street has already moved higher, but in our view it still underestimates how excess cash can translate into upgraded shareholder distributions.

Finally, valuation also remains supportive. Relative to the wider market, the sector's FCF yield remains above its historical average, suggesting that the equity market is still not fully pricing the improved cash flow outlook

This leaves European Energy in a different investment phase. The sector can compound through a combination of resilient free cash flow, balance sheet repair and rising shareholder distributions, while still offering a hedge against persistent macro and geopolitical disruption. That combination is not fully priced, in our view. We therefore maintain our Attractive sector view for the European Energy Majors.
On a stock level, our preferences also remain unchanged for the time, and we like TotalEnergies, BP and Repsol to play the sector:
TotalEnergies (Overweight, Top Pick): TotalEnergies remains our preferred quality compounder in the sector. Its oil and gas portfolio provides sector-leading growth while its

Integrated Power adds a differentiated FCF growth leg in the medium term. Price-conditioned distributions and ongoing capital discipline give the company flexibility through the cycle, making the investment case less dependent on a single commodity outcome.

BP (Overweight): BP offers the highest torque to the stronger commodity backdrop among the European majors, with oil, gas and refining upside feeding directly into de-gearing capacity and the potential recovery of distributions over time. The investment case is also helped by a self-help agenda that is becoming more tangible with strong operational performance. On our numbers, the shares screen particularly compelling with FCF yield of ~13% (post-leases and hybrids) in an oil scenario of $80/bbl, driving valuation support alongside the macro leverage.

Repsol (Overweight): After a hiccup in early April, refining margins have recovered in Europe in recent weeks, and we expect Repsol to be nimble to monetise that opportunity at its diesel-leveraged plants. Supported by that, we see the stock trading at a discount to peers at  \( >16\% \)  clean FCF yield this year, which should allow it to raise the pace of share buybacks over the coming quarters.

Macro-political developments leading to the potential implementation of windfall taxes are key to follow in this case. However, if history is any guide, we do not currently expect a potential taxation increase to affect the company's ability to remunerate shareholders (see Exploring the Impact of Potential Windfall Taxes), and therefore remain Overweight.

Shell (Equal-weight): Shell is a defensive business, supported by balance sheet strength and a broad earnings mix. However, those attributes are less differentiated in a stronger commodity tape, where higher-beta peers offer greater upside capture. The potential acquisition of ARC helps address a growth shortfall to peers, but, after incorporating producing assets, Shell's forward-looking annual growth of ~1% remains less compelling than that of TotalEnergies or Eni.

Equinor (Equal-weight): Equinor has clear upside to tighter oil and gas markets, given its high sensitivity to European gas prices and its relatively low exposure to Middle East asset disruption. On the other hand, beyond the short-term disruption, the medium-term equity story still leaves open questions around capital allocation – specifically, how the company will be able to diversify away from a declining Norwegian Continental Shelf. With those opportunities and risks broadly balanced, the shares look more fairly positioned after the recent re-rating.

Eni (Equal-weight): Eni offers high production growth, high commodity beta and a clear strategic framework through its satellite model. The stronger commodity backdrop supports cash generation and buybacks, while recent execution has reinforced confidence in the growth story. However, the valuation already reflects much of that progress, leaving the shares less attractive than other high-beta or quality-compounding opportunities in the sector.

Galp (Equal-weight): We continue to like Galp's long-term value proposition with a high-quality portfolio of oil & gas fields in Brazil and Namibia, and think the potential combination of downstream assets with Moeve could drive interest from the market to the shares (for more details on the ongoing discussions see What We Know About the Galp/Moeve Downstream Combination). However, for the time being, we continue to find
Galp's story too defensive relative to other opportunities in our sector (such as Repsol), and hence remain on the sidelines.
